validation.notes: Items curated for Teacher Israel Ventura class guided practice and future mocks. Original workplace English only (not ETS material). Intro set (TQB-P5-0001–0010) remains separate and unchanged. Lote 1 added TQB-P5-0051–0070; Lote 2 added TQB-P5-0071–0090; Lote 3 added TQB-P5-0091–0110; Lote 4 added TQB-P5-0111–0130; Lote 5 added TQB-P5-0131–0150 (20 items) toward ~200-item class bank.

items.question: Customers praised the _____ of the support staff after the system outage.
items.explanation: The blank needs a noun after "the." "Professionalism" is the noun that names the quality.
items.commonMistake: "Professional" is an adjective and cannot follow "the" as the object of praised.
items.learningObjective: After the + of, look for a noun naming a quality or action.

items.question: The warehouse supervisor asked for a written _____ of each delayed shipment.
items.explanation: After "a written," a noun is required. "Explanation" names the document requested.
items.commonMistake: "Explanatory" is an adjective; "explain" is a verb.
items.learningObjective: Choose a noun when a determiner and adjective precede the blank.

items.question: After the product launch, client feedback was surprisingly _____.
items.explanation: After the linking verb "was," an adjective describes the subject. "Favorable" is correct.
items.commonMistake: "Favorably" is an adverb and does not follow a linking verb as a subject complement.
items.learningObjective: After be/seem/appear, choose an adjective, not an adverb.

items.question: The audit committee issued a _____ report recommending tighter expense controls.
items.explanation: The blank modifies "report," so an adjective is needed. "Conclusive" means decisive or definitive.
items.commonMistake: "Conclusion" is a noun; "conclusively" is an adverb.
items.learningObjective: Match word form to the slot: adjective before noun.

items.question: When the fire alarm sounded, the accounting team _____ the monthly close.
items.explanation: A longer action was in progress when a shorter past event interrupted it. Past continuous fits.
items.commonMistake: Simple present or present perfect do not describe a past-in-progress scene.
items.learningObjective: When + past event, past continuous for the background action.

items.question: The help desk _____ ticket volume since the software upgrade began last week.
items.explanation: "Since" plus a continuing action calls for present perfect continuous: "has been monitoring."
items.commonMistake: Simple past "monitored" does not show an action still ongoing from a past starting point.
items.learningObjective: Use present perfect continuous with since/for for actions that started in the past and continue.

items.question: By the time the shuttle arrived, most passengers _____ already checked in online.
items.explanation: Past perfect places the online check-in before another past event (the shuttle's arrival): "had already checked."
items.commonMistake: Choosing present perfect "have" when both events are clearly finished in the past.
items.learningObjective: Use past perfect for the earlier of two past actions.

items.question: According to the agenda, Mr. Chen _____ introduce the new vendors after lunch.
items.explanation: A planned future action on an agenda uses "is going to" + base verb: "is going to introduce."
items.commonMistake: Using present simple "goes" without marking a planned future introduction.
items.learningObjective: Mark planned future workplace actions with be going to.

items.question: Ms. Patel is responsible _____ coordinating the intern orientation in June.
items.explanation: The collocation is "responsible for" + noun/gerund.
items.commonMistake: "Responsible of" is a common transfer error from other languages.
items.learningObjective: Learn adjective + preposition pairs as chunks.

items.question: Expense reports must be filed _____ the last business day of each month.
items.explanation: "By" means "no later than" a deadline. Filing should be complete on or before that day.
items.commonMistake: "Until" describes a continuing state, not a completion deadline. "During" needs a period, not a single day as a cutoff.
items.learningObjective: Use by for the latest acceptable time to finish something.

items.question: Ms. Rivera is in charge _____ booking conference rooms for visiting clients.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is "in charge of" + gerund/noun.
items.commonMistake: "In charge to" confuses this phrase with "responsible to" (a person).
items.learningObjective: Use of after in charge when naming a duty.

items.question: _____ the projector failed, the presenter continued using printed handouts.
items.explanation: "Although" introduces a full clause (subject + verb). "The projector failed" is a clause.
items.commonMistake: "Despite" and "because of" need a noun phrase, not a full sentence. "However" cannot start this pattern without punctuation changes.
items.learningObjective: Although/while/because + clause; despite/because of + noun.

items.question: The proposal was well researched; _____, the board postponed a final vote.
items.explanation: The second clause contrasts with the first, so "however" is the right transition.
items.commonMistake: "Therefore" signals result, not contrast.
items.learningObjective: Use however to mark unexpected contrast between clauses.

items.question: Agents save call notes carefully _____ supervisors can review unresolved cases later.
items.explanation: "So that" introduces purpose: notes are saved to enable later review.
items.commonMistake: "Even if" introduces a concessive condition, not purpose.
items.learningObjective: Use so that to show purpose between two clauses.

items.question: The supervisor _____ approved the overtime request is out of the office today.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of "approved," so "who" is correct.
items.commonMistake: "Whom" is for objects. If you can replace it with he/she, use who.
items.learningObjective: Who = subject; whom = object; whose = possessive.

items.question: Please contact the representative _____ territory includes the western districts.
items.explanation: "Whose" shows possession linking the representative to "territory."
items.commonMistake: "Who" cannot mark possession before a noun like "territory."
items.learningObjective: Use whose for possessive relative clauses about people.

items.question: Mr. Haddad reserved the hotel room _____, without using the travel desk.
items.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is needed when the subject and object are the same person: "himself."
items.commonMistake: "Him" would imply a different person reserved the room for Mr. Haddad.
items.learningObjective: Use reflexive pronouns for actions done by the subject to/for the subject.

items.question: The warehouse manager, along with two clerks, _____ preparing the inventory count.
items.explanation: Phrases like "along with" do not change the subject. The subject is "manager" (singular): "is."
items.commonMistake: Learners agree with "clerks" because it is closer. Cover the middle phrase and re-read.
items.learningObjective: Along with / together with / as well as do not make a singular subject plural.

items.question: Neither the brochure nor the price list _____ the new warranty terms.
items.explanation: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "Price list" is singular, so "mentions."
items.commonMistake: People choose a plural verb because two things are named. Agreement follows the nearest noun.
items.learningObjective: Neither A nor B → verb matches B.

items.question: Each of the applicants _____ required to submit a writing sample.
items.explanation: "Each" is singular, so the verb is "is" even though "applicants" is plural.
items.commonMistake: Agreeing with "applicants" instead of with "each."
items.learningObjective: Treat each/every as singular subjects.

items.question: Either the drivers or the dispatcher _____ the load sheets before departure.
items.explanation: With either…or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject "dispatcher" (singular): "signs."
items.commonMistake: Agreeing with "drivers" instead of the subject closest to the verb.
items.learningObjective: In either…or / neither…nor, agree with the nearest noun.

items.question: If we _____ a larger warehouse, we could keep more stock on site.
items.explanation: An unreal present situation uses if + past, then would/could + base verb.
items.commonMistake: "If we have" is first conditional (real). "Would have" does not belong in the if-clause.
items.learningObjective: Second conditional: if + past, would/could + verb.

items.question: If the flight had been canceled, the team _____ the meeting by video.
items.explanation: A past unreal condition (had been canceled) pairs with would have + past participle.
items.commonMistake: "Would join" is second conditional (present unreal), not a finished past event.
items.learningObjective: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.

items.question: If the printer _____ working, staff would not need to walk to another floor.
items.explanation: Second conditional uses past form in the if-clause; "were" is standard for unreal present.
items.commonMistake: Using present "is" would make a first conditional, which needs "will" not "would."
items.learningObjective: Second conditional: if + past, would + base verb.

items.question: Bonus payments _____ into staff accounts on the last Friday of March.
items.explanation: Payments are the object of the action. Future passive: will be deposited.
items.commonMistake: "Will deposit" is active and needs a depositor as subject.
items.learningObjective: Future passive = will be + past participle.

items.question: The minutes of Tuesday's planning session _____ on the shared drive.
items.explanation: The minutes received the action, and the result matters now: have been posted.
items.commonMistake: "Have posted" is active; minutes do not post themselves.
items.learningObjective: Present perfect passive = have/has been + past participle.

items.question: New ID badges _____ printed in the security office this afternoon.
items.explanation: Present continuous passive is "are being" + past participle for an action in progress.
items.commonMistake: "Are printed" is present simple passive and misses the ongoing sense of "this afternoon."
items.learningObjective: Use am/is/are being + PP for passive actions happening now.

items.question: This year's catalog is not _____ colorful as the holiday edition.
items.explanation: The structure is as + adjective + as. "Not as colorful as" is the full pattern.
items.commonMistake: "More colorful as" mixes comparative and equative forms. Use more … than, or as … as.
items.learningObjective: Equality (or its negative) uses as + adj + as.

items.question: The revised budget includes _____ travel days than last quarter's plan.
items.explanation: "Days" is countable, so "fewer" is the correct comparative.
items.commonMistake: "Less" is for uncountable nouns (less time, less money). Travel days can be counted.
items.learningObjective: Fewer + countable plural; less + uncountable.

items.question: Among the three vendors, Apex offered the _____ competitive annual fee.
items.explanation: Comparing three vendors requires the superlative "the most competitive."
items.commonMistake: "More" is for comparing only two things.
items.learningObjective: Use the most + adj when ranking three or more options.

items.question: We look forward to _____ you at the product showcase next month.
items.explanation: In "look forward to," to is a preposition, so a gerund follows: meeting.
items.commonMistake: Learners treat to as an infinitive marker and choose "meet." Here to is not the infinitive.
items.learningObjective: After a preposition (including to in look forward to), use verb-ing.

items.question: Please avoid _____ large files as attachments; use the shared folder instead.
items.explanation: Avoid is followed by a gerund: avoid sending.
items.commonMistake: Avoid to send is a frequent error. After avoid, enjoy, finish, keep — use -ing.
items.learningObjective: Avoid + verb-ing.

items.question: Managers suggested _____ the wellness survey before the holiday break.
items.explanation: "Suggest" is followed by a gerund: "suggested distributing."
items.commonMistake: "Suggest to distribute" mirrors other verbs incorrectly; suggest takes -ing.
items.learningObjective: After suggest/recommend/avoid, use a gerund.

items.question: New interns are not yet used to _____ in an open-plan workspace.
items.explanation: "Be used to" means accustomed to and is followed by a gerund or noun.
items.commonMistake: Confusing "be used to + -ing" with "used to + base verb" (past habit).
items.learningObjective: After be/get used to, use a gerund.

items.question: Please take _____ elevator on the left to reach the executive suite.
items.explanation: A specific elevator is identified ("on the left"), so "the" is required.
items.commonMistake: "A elevator" is also wrong because elevator begins with a vowel sound; but the real issue is specificity.
items.learningObjective: Use the when the listener can identify which one.

items.question: If this pallet is damaged, please request _____ one from the staging area.
items.explanation: "Another" means one additional singular countable item: "another one."
items.commonMistake: "Other" needs a plural noun or "the other" for a specific remaining item.
items.learningObjective: Use another before singular countable nouns.

items.question: Please book _____ earliest flight that arrives before the afternoon workshop.
items.explanation: Superlatives take "the": "the earliest flight."
items.commonMistake: Omitting the article or using "a/an" before a superlative adjective + noun.
items.learningObjective: Use the before superlative adjective + noun.

items.question: Visitors _____ enter the server room without an escort from IT.
items.explanation: "Must not" forbids an action. The rule bans unescorted entry.
items.commonMistake: "Need" requires "to" and does not by itself mean prohibition. "Ought" needs "to" as well.
items.learningObjective: Must not = it is not allowed.

items.question: Accountants _____ to attach receipts when they submit mileage claims.
items.explanation: "Have to" expresses external obligation; the blank needs "have" before "to attach."
items.commonMistake: "Must to" is ungrammatical; must is followed by a bare infinitive.
items.learningObjective: Recognize have to as a modal-like obligation form.

items.question: The team _____ have confirmed the dial-in code before inviting external guests.
items.explanation: "Should have" + past participle criticizes a past action that was advisable but not done.
items.commonMistake: "Must have" expresses deduction about the past, not regretful advice.
items.learningObjective: Distinguish should have (past advice/regret) from must have (past deduction).

items.question: The new scheduling software is compatible _____ both desktop and mobile devices.
items.explanation: The adjective "compatible" takes the preposition "with." The blank needs "with" before the devices named.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "to" by analogy with "similar to." Compatible pairs with "with," not "to."
items.learningObjective: Memorize adjective + preposition pairs: compatible with.

items.question: Employees are prohibited _____ using personal devices inside the clean room.
items.explanation: "Prohibited from" is the fixed pattern before a gerund. The blank requires "from."
items.commonMistake: Selecting "against" (closer to "protect against") or "for," which do not follow "prohibited."
items.learningObjective: After prohibited/prevented/banned, expect from + -ing.

items.question: Production slowed last week; _____, overtime costs rose sharply.
items.explanation: The second clause is a result of the first. "Consequently" signals cause → effect between independent clauses.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "moreover" (adds information) or "meanwhile" (simultaneous time), which do not show result.
items.learningObjective: Match transitions to meaning: result → consequently / therefore / as a result.

items.question: _____ the vendor lowers its unit price, purchasing will seek another supplier.
items.explanation: "Unless" means "if not." The company will look elsewhere if the vendor does not lower the price.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "Although" (contrast) or "Because/Since" (reason), which reverse or change the logic.
items.learningObjective: Treat unless as a connector meaning if not — not as a verb-tense conditional item.

items.question: The handbook explains how employees can update _____ emergency contacts online.
items.explanation: A possessive determiner is needed before the noun "emergency contacts." "Their" fills that slot.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "theirs" (standalone possessive) or "them" (object pronoun), which cannot modify a noun.
items.learningObjective: Before a noun, use my/your/their — not mine/yours/theirs.

items.question: The specialist _____ the board hired last month will present the findings on Friday.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the object of "hired" (the board hired the specialist), so "whom" is correct.
items.commonMistake: Defaulting to "who" because it appears before the verb "will present." Check the relative clause role first.
items.learningObjective: Who = subject; whom = object; whose = possession; which = things.

items.question: If demand _____ next quarter, the plant will add a second shift.
items.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base verb. "Increases" matches the real future plan.
items.commonMistake: Using "would increase" or past forms, which belong to unreal (second/third) conditionals.
items.learningObjective: Real future: If + present, will + V.

items.question: If management _____ more notice, staff could have rearranged their schedules.
items.explanation: Third conditional looks back at an unreal past: If + past perfect ("had given"), modal perfect in the result ("could have rearranged").
items.commonMistake: Choosing simple past "gave," which fits second conditional, not a past counterfactual with "could have."
items.learningObjective: Unreal past: If + had + V3, would/could have + V3.

items.question: All refund requests _____ carefully before a credit is issued.
items.explanation: The requests receive the action; no agent is needed. Present simple passive: are + past participle.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the active "review," which would need a plural human subject performing the action.
items.learningObjective: When the object is the subject, use be + past participle.

items.question: By Friday, the quarterly forecasts _____ to every department head.
items.explanation: "By Friday" marks a deadline in the future for a completed action on the forecasts → future perfect passive: will have been + V3.
items.commonMistake: Choosing active "will distribute," which needs a subject who distributes, or mixing progressive forms.
items.learningObjective: By + future time + completed action on object → will have been + past participle.

items.question: Online modules are _____ expensive than sending staff to off-site seminars.
items.explanation: Comparing two options with an adjective uses "less … than." "Fewer" is for countable nouns, not adjectives.
items.commonMistake: Selecting "fewer" because costs feel countable, or "least," which is a superlative without a comparison group.
items.learningObjective: less + adj/uncountable; fewer + plural countable; least/most for superlatives.

items.question: Of all the proposals submitted, Nexus offered the _____ delivery timeline.
items.explanation: "Of all the proposals" signals a superlative among many. Short → shorter → shortest.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the comparative "shorter," which compares only two things, or the adverb "shortly."
items.learningObjective: Of all / among + group → the + -est / most.

items.question: The hiring manager holds _____ MBA from a well-known business school.
items.explanation: "MBA" begins with a vowel sound (/em/), so the indefinite article is "an."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "a" by looking at the letter M as a consonant letter rather than its spoken sound.
items.learningObjective: Choose a/an by sound, not spelling: an hour, an MBA, a university.

items.question: There is _____ time left to revise the slides before the client call.
items.explanation: "Time" is uncountable, so "little" (not "few/many/several") is the correct determiner for a small amount.
items.commonMistake: Using "few" or "several," which modify plural countable nouns, not uncountable "time."
items.learningObjective: little/much + uncountable; few/many + plural countable.

items.question: Staff _____ wear closed-toe shoes when touring the production floor.
items.explanation: Safety rules express strong obligation. "Must" is the fitting modal before the base verb "wear."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "can" (ability/permission) or "might" (possibility), which weaken a required safety rule.
items.learningObjective: Must = strong obligation; can/might = ability or possibility.

items.question: You _____ better double-check the account numbers before transferring funds.
items.explanation: The fixed advice pattern is "had better + base verb." Here "had" completes "had better double-check."
items.commonMistake: Inserting "should" or "would" before "better," which produces ungrammatical strings in standard workplace English.
items.learningObjective: had better + V = strong advice / warning.

items.question: The CEO's _____ remarks opened the annual shareholders' meeting.
items.explanation: The blank modifies the noun "remarks," so an adjective is required: "introductory."
items.commonMistake: Choosing the noun "introduction" or the verb "introduce," which cannot modify "remarks" in this slot.
items.learningObjective: Adjective + noun: look for -ive/-ory/-al forms before the head noun.

items.question: Rapid _____ in the logistics sector has created new warehouse jobs.
items.explanation: After the adjective "Rapid," the subject needs a noun: "growth." The verb "has created" confirms a noun subject.
items.commonMistake: Selecting "growing" (participle/gerund) when a plain noun subject is required after "Rapid."
items.learningObjective: Adj + noun subject: Rapid growth / Strong demand / High turnover.

items.question: Right now, the IT crew _____ the new printers on the third floor.
items.explanation: "Right now" marks an action in progress. Present continuous: is/are + -ing.
items.commonMistake: Choosing present simple "installs" (habits) or present perfect (completed result), which ignore "right now."
items.learningObjective: Time markers like right now / currently → present continuous.

items.question: By the time the auditor arrives tomorrow, the clerks _____ the ledgers twice.
items.explanation: Future perfect shows an action finished before a future point: will have + past participle before "the auditor arrives."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "will review," which does not guarantee completion before the arrival time marker.
items.learningObjective: By the time + present, will have + V3.

items.question: The number of remote positions _____ increased significantly since last year.
items.explanation: With "the number of," the head noun is singular "number," so the verb is singular: has.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "have" because "positions" is plural; agreement follows "number," not the plural noun after of.
items.learningObjective: Use a singular verb after "the number of + plural noun."

items.question: Everyone in the sales department _____ required to attend Thursday's product briefing.
items.explanation: Indefinite pronouns like everyone take a singular verb. "Is required" matches the singular subject.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "are" because many people are implied; grammatically everyone is singular.
items.learningObjective: Match singular verbs to everyone, everybody, someone, and similar pronouns.

items.subskill: One of the + plural + singular verb
items.question: One of the proposals _____ a detailed timeline for the warehouse expansion.
items.explanation: In "one of the + plural noun," the subject is singular "one," so the verb is includes.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "include" to agree with "proposals"; the true subject is "one."
items.learningObjective: After "one of the + plural noun," use a third-person singular verb.

items.question: After reviewing the quotes, purchasing decided _____ with a local supplier.
items.explanation: Decide is followed by a to-infinitive: decided to proceed.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the bare infinitive "proceed" or the gerund "proceeding," which do not follow decide.
items.learningObjective: After decide, use to + base verb.

items.question: Would you mind _____ the conference call by fifteen minutes?
items.explanation: Mind takes a gerund: Would you mind rescheduling…?
items.commonMistake: Choosing "to reschedule" because many polite requests use infinitives; mind requires verb-ing.
items.learningObjective: After mind (and would you mind), use a gerund.

items.question: Several tenants objected to _____ the lobby renovated during business hours.
items.explanation: In "object to," to is a preposition, so a gerund follows: objected to having…
items.commonMistake: Treating to as an infinitive marker and choosing "have" or "to have."
items.learningObjective: After object to (and similar verb + to preposition patterns), use verb-ing.

items.question: The courier delivered the contract _____ so that the signing could begin on time.
items.explanation: The blank modifies the verb delivered, so an adverb is needed: promptly.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the adjective "prompt," which cannot modify a verb.
items.learningObjective: Use an -ly adverb when the blank modifies how an action is done.

items.question: Regular _____ of equipment reduces unexpected downtime on the production line.
items.explanation: After the adjective Regular, the blank needs a noun subject: maintenance.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the verb "maintain" or the participle "maintaining," which cannot fill a noun slot after Regular.
items.learningObjective: After an adjective before of + noun phrase, select the matching noun form.

items.question: The facilities crew _____ the air filters in every conference room two weeks ago.
items.explanation: "Two weeks ago" marks a finished past time, so simple past replaced is required.
items.commonMistake: Choosing present perfect "have replaced," which does not pair with ago + specific past time.
items.learningObjective: Use simple past with finished-time markers such as ago, yesterday, and last week.

items.question: At this time tomorrow, the inspectors _____ the loading docks.
items.explanation: "At this time tomorrow" points to an action in progress in the future: will be visiting.
items.commonMistake: Choosing simple "visit" or present perfect; the time phrase needs future continuous.
items.learningObjective: Use will be + -ing for actions in progress at a future moment.

items.question: Managers should be aware _____ seasonal spikes in customer complaints.
items.explanation: The adjective aware is paired with of: aware of seasonal spikes.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "to" or "for," which fit other adjectives (accustomed to, responsible for) but not aware.
items.learningObjective: Memorize adjective + preposition pairs such as aware of.

items.question: The upgraded scanner is capable _____ processing double-sided forms automatically.
items.explanation: Capable takes of + gerund: capable of processing…
items.commonMistake: Choosing "to" by analogy with able to; capable uses of, not to.
items.learningObjective: Use capable of + verb-ing (contrast with able to + base verb).

items.question: The venue is centrally located; _____, it offers complimentary parking for guests.
items.explanation: Moreover adds a second advantage after a semicolon: it is an additive transition adverb.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "although" or "despite," which signal contrast, or "because," which needs a reason clause.
items.learningObjective: Use moreover / furthermore to add supporting information between clauses.

items.question: Please open the spreadsheet _____ contains last quarter's shipping totals.
items.explanation: Which refers to things (the spreadsheet) and acts as the subject of contains.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "who" (people) or "whose" (possession) instead of which for a thing subject.
items.learningObjective: Use which (or that) for non-human antecedents in relative clauses.

items.question: If the temperature _____ above 30°C, the cooling system activates automatically.
items.explanation: Zero conditionals use present simple in both clauses for general truths: If … rises, … activates.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "will rise" as if it were a first conditional; the result clause is also present simple.
items.learningObjective: For routines and automatic results, use present simple in the if-clause (zero conditional).

items.question: The updated safety manual _____ to every shift supervisor last Monday.
items.explanation: The manual received the action in the past: was distributed (past simple passive).
items.commonMistake: Choosing active "distributed" without an agent subject, or malformed "has distributing."
items.learningObjective: Form past simple passive with was/were + past participle.

items.question: Please review the invoice _____ carefully than you did last time.
items.explanation: The comparison marker than requires comparative more carefully (not most).
items.commonMistake: Choosing "most" (superlative) or "much," which does not form the comparative with carefully + than.
items.learningObjective: Use more + adverb + than for adverb comparatives.

items.question: Please use _____ other entrance while the main lobby is being painted.
items.explanation: "The other" points to a specific remaining alternative among known options.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "a"/"an" (another pattern) or "any"; here the alternative entrance is definite.
items.learningObjective: Use the other for a definite remaining option; contrast with another.

items.question: Shipping _____ be delayed if the storm reaches the coastal ports tonight.
items.explanation: Might expresses possibility: shipping might be delayed.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "had better" or "must not," which express advice or prohibition, not possibility.
items.learningObjective: Use might/may for uncertain future outcomes.

items.question: With clearer instructions, the contractors _____ the wiring sooner.
items.explanation: Could have + past participle expresses an unreal past ability/opportunity: they could have finished sooner (but did not).
items.commonMistake: Choosing present/future modals (can/must/will finish) that ignore the unreal past meaning.
items.learningObjective: Use could have + past participle for missed past possibilities.

items.question: Retail sales fell slightly in May; _____, online orders continued to climb.
items.explanation: Nevertheless signals contrast between two independent clauses joined by a semicolon: sales fell, but online orders rose.
items.commonMistake: Choosing because or so that, which express cause or purpose rather than contrast.
items.learningObjective: Use nevertheless for contrast after a semicolon.

items.question: Full-time staff receive stock options, _____ temporary contractors do not.
items.explanation: Whereas contrasts two clauses: full-time employees get options, but contractors do not.
items.commonMistake: Choosing therefore (result) or furthermore (addition) instead of a contrast connector.
items.learningObjective: Use whereas to contrast two clauses in workplace comparisons.

items.question: Please renew your password before Friday; _____, your account will be locked.
items.explanation: Otherwise means 'if not': renew the password, or your account will be locked.
items.commonMistake: Selecting although (concession) or likewise (similarity), which do not signal a negative consequence.
items.learningObjective: Use otherwise to show what happens if the first action is not taken.

items.question: The company prides _____ on responding to customer complaints within 24 hours.
items.explanation: Pride oneself on requires a reflexive: the company (singular inanimate) → itself.
items.commonMistake: Using it or its after pride, which need a reflexive object matching the subject.
items.learningObjective: Match reflexive pronouns to singular company/organization subjects.

items.question: New hires should introduce _____ to their mentors during the first week.
items.explanation: Introduce requires a reflexive when the subject and object are the same people: new hires → themselves.
items.commonMistake: Choosing them (object pronoun) instead of the reflexive themselves.
items.learningObjective: Use themselves when plural subjects act on themselves.

items.question: Please forward any billing questions to the accountant _____ invoices are routinely sent.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the object of the preposition to (invoices are sent to someone) → to whom.
items.commonMistake: Choosing who (subject form) or whose (possessive) when the blank needs a preposition + object relative.
items.learningObjective: Use to whom when the relative is the object of a stranded/fronted preposition.

items.question: If the building inspection passes tomorrow, renovations _____ the following week.
items.explanation: First conditional: present in the if-clause (passes) + will + base verb in the result clause.
items.commonMistake: Using would have begun (third conditional) or began (past) for a real future result.
items.learningObjective: Pair a present if-clause with will + base verb for likely future results.

items.question: If the plant operated around the clock, overtime costs _____ significantly.
items.explanation: Second conditional (unreal present): past-form if-clause (operated) + would + base verb in the result.
items.commonMistake: Choosing will rise, which belongs in a first-conditional (real future) result clause.
items.learningObjective: Use would + base verb after an unreal present if-clause.

items.question: _____ the auditor arrived earlier, the duplicate payment would have been caught.
items.explanation: Inverted third conditional omits if: Had + subject + past participle (= If the auditor had arrived). The result uses would have + pp.
items.commonMistake: Putting If alone without had, or Were/Should which invert different conditional types.
items.learningObjective: Recognize Had + subject + pp as an inverted third-conditional if-clause.

items.question: All expense claims _____ by a department manager before reimbursement.
items.explanation: Modal passive: modal + be + past participle. Claims are the object of approve, so they must be approved.
items.commonMistake: Using must approve (active) when the subject (claims) does not perform the action.
items.learningObjective: Form modal passives with modal + be + past participle.

items.question: By the time the warehouse opened, the damaged crates _____ to the supplier.
items.explanation: Past perfect passive (had been + pp) shows an action completed before another past event (warehouse opened).
items.commonMistake: Choosing have returned (active present perfect) or will be returned (future) with a past time anchor.
items.learningObjective: Use had been + past participle for passive actions before a past reference point.

items.question: The lobby elevators _____ serviced when visitors arrived for the open house.
items.explanation: Past continuous passive: were being + past participle (serviced) for an action in progress at a past moment.
items.commonMistake: Choosing are being (present) or have been (present perfect) when the when-clause is past narrative.
items.learningObjective: Form past continuous passives with was/were being + past participle.

items.question: Independent tests show that Model B performs _____ than Model A in humid climates.
items.explanation: Comparative better + than compares two models. Best is superlative; good/well lack the comparative form needed with than.
items.commonMistake: Choosing best (superlative) when only two things are compared with than.
items.learningObjective: Use better than for two-item comparisons of performance.

items.question: Among the four shipping options, ground freight is the _____ expensive for bulk orders.
items.explanation: With among + a group of more than two, use the least + adjective for the lowest degree.
items.commonMistake: Using less (comparative for two) when the stem compares among four options.
items.learningObjective: Use the least + adjective for superlative low degree among three or more.

items.question: Interest rates this quarter are _____ than they were at the start of the year.
items.explanation: Comparative higher + than compares two time points. Highest needs the + among a group; high/highly are not comparative.
items.commonMistake: Selecting highest without the and a multi-item group, or highly (adverb) before than.
items.learningObjective: Use -er comparatives with than for two-point comparisons.

items.question: _____ few seats remain in the front row for tomorrow's shareholder briefing.
items.explanation: A few + plural countable noun means a small positive number. An does not fit before few; much is for uncountables.
items.commonMistake: Confusing a few (some) with few alone (almost none), or choosing much with a countable plural.
items.learningObjective: Use a few before plural countables to mean a small number.

items.question: _____ employee must submit a timesheet by 5:00 p.m. on Friday.
items.explanation: Each takes a singular countable noun (employee) and a singular verb (must). All/Many need plurals; Both needs exactly two.
items.commonMistake: Choosing All with a singular noun instead of All employees.
items.learningObjective: Use each before a singular noun when referring to every individual in a group.

items.question: It was _____ a long delay that several passengers requested meal vouchers.
items.explanation: Such a + adjective + singular noun + that expresses degree: such a long delay that… So would need so long a delay / so long that.
items.commonMistake: Choosing so, which patterns as so + adjective (+ that), not so a + noun.
items.learningObjective: Use such a/an before adjective + singular noun in degree clauses.

items.question: Several applicants were interested _____ relocating to the regional office.
items.explanation: The adjective interested is followed by in (+ noun/gerund): interested in relocating.
items.commonMistake: Using interested on/at/for, which are not standard collocations with interested.
items.learningObjective: Remember the fixed collocation interested in.

items.question: The organizers _____ to have reserved a larger hall for the annual awards dinner.
items.explanation: Ought to have + past participle criticizes a past action not taken. The stem already includes to have reserved, so only ought fits.
items.commonMistake: Choosing must/can/may, which do not form must to have / can to have in this advice pattern.
items.learningObjective: Use ought to have + pp for past advice or mild criticism.

items.question: A number of employees _____ volunteered to mentor the incoming summer interns.
items.explanation: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb. "Have volunteered" agrees with the plural sense of employees.
items.commonMistake: Learners confuse "a number of" (plural) with "the number of" (singular) and choose "has."
items.learningObjective: Use a plural verb after "a number of + plural noun."

items.question: The chief financial officer, as well as the junior analysts, _____ attending the budget hearing on Monday.
items.explanation: Phrases with "as well as" do not change the subject. The singular subject "officer" requires "is."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "are" because "analysts" is nearer and plural.
items.learningObjective: Ignore "as well as" phrases when matching subject and verb.

items.question: The new laboratory equipment _____ scheduled for delivery before the research wing opens.
items.explanation: "Equipment" is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb even when it refers to many machines.
items.commonMistake: Treating "equipment" as plural because it names multiple devices.
items.learningObjective: Use singular verbs with uncountable workplace nouns like equipment, information, and news.

items.question: Every visitor who enters the restricted wing _____ a temporary badge at the security desk.
items.explanation: "Every" makes the subject singular, so the verb must be "receives" even though "who enters" describes visitors.
items.commonMistake: Matching the verb to "visitors" in meaning and choosing the plural "receive."
items.learningObjective: After "every + singular noun," use a third-person singular verb.

items.question: The plant manager is considering _____ a night shift to clear the order backlog.
items.explanation: "Consider" is followed by a gerund when it means thinking about an action: considering adding.
items.commonMistake: Using "to add" because many verbs of planning take infinitives.
items.learningObjective: Use a gerund after consider when naming a possible action.

items.question: Regional managers expect _____ the revised commission plan before the next quarter begins.
items.explanation: "Expect" takes a to-infinitive when stating what someone anticipates doing or getting: expect to receive.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the gerund "receiving," which fits verbs like "anticipate" or "look forward to."
items.learningObjective: Use to-infinitive after expect + object-less pattern.

items.question: Because key stakeholders were traveling, the committee postponed _____ the merger vote.
items.explanation: "Postpone" is followed by a gerund: postponed holding. Infinitives are not used after postpone.
items.commonMistake: Selecting "to hold" by analogy with "decide to" or "plan to."
items.learningObjective: Use a gerund after postpone, delay, and similar verbs of deferring.

items.question: Our firm remains committed to _____ packaging waste across all product lines by 2028.
items.explanation: In "committed to," the word "to" is a preposition, so it takes a gerund: committed to reducing.
items.commonMistake: Treating "to" as the infinitive marker and choosing "reduce."
items.learningObjective: After adjective + to (preposition), use a gerund, not a bare infinitive.

items.question: The campaign results were _____ better than the agency had projected in April.
items.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the comparative adjective "better." "Significantly" is the adverb form.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the adjective "significant," which cannot modify another adjective.
items.learningObjective: Use an adverb before a comparative adjective to show degree.

items.question: Legal counsel requested a full _____ of the contractor's insurance coverage before signing.
items.explanation: After "a full," the blank needs a noun. "Disclosure" is the noun naming the act of revealing information.
items.commonMistake: Selecting the verb "disclose" because it looks related to the legal context.
items.learningObjective: Recognize noun slots after article + adjective.

items.question: Complaint volume _____ steadily since the self-service portal launched in March.
items.explanation: "Since" plus a past starting point signals present perfect for a change that continues to matter now: has declined.
items.commonMistake: Using simple past "declined," which does not connect the change to the present.
items.learningObjective: Pair present perfect with since + starting time.

items.question: By the time the patch was released, technicians _____ the network issue for nearly six hours.
items.explanation: Past perfect continuous shows an action in progress up to a past moment ("by the time the patch was released").
items.commonMistake: Choosing present perfect continuous, which cannot sit before a finished past time marker.
items.learningObjective: Use had been + -ing for duration before a past reference point.

items.question: The launch date will depend _____ how quickly the suppliers can fulfill the rush order.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is "depend on" (or "upon"). Other prepositions are incorrect here.
items.commonMistake: Saying "depend of," a transfer error from Spanish "depender de."
items.learningObjective: Memorize depend on as the standard workplace preposition pattern.

items.question: All supervisors are expected to participate _____ the two-day leadership workshop in October.
items.explanation: "Participate" takes the preposition "in" before an event or activity: participate in the workshop.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "on" or "at," which fit other verbs (focus on, arrive at) but not participate.
items.learningObjective: Use participate in + activity/event.

items.question: Contractors _____ to complete the online safety quiz before they may enter the site.
items.explanation: "Need to" expresses obligation. With a plural subject, the form is "need to complete."
items.commonMistake: Using "needs" to agree with a singular idea of "each contractor" when the subject is plural.
items.learningObjective: Use need to + base verb for workplace requirements.

items.question: The refrigerated shipment _____ to arrive before noon, but the truck is still two hours away.
items.explanation: "Be supposed to" marks an expected plan. Past "was supposed to" fits because the expected arrival time has already passed relative to the contrast.
items.commonMistake: Dropping the auxiliary and writing "supposed to" without "was/is."
items.learningObjective: Use be supposed to for scheduled expectations, with tense matching the time frame.

items.question: The downtown branch offers extended hours; _____, it provides free notary services to account holders.
items.explanation: "Furthermore" adds a second positive point after a semicolon, matching the additive relationship between the two clauses.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "instead," which signals replacement rather than addition.
items.learningObjective: Use furthermore to add supporting information between independent clauses.

items.question: Their proposal is longer, but _____ includes clearer cost estimates for the renovation.
items.explanation: The blank stands alone as the subject of "includes," so the independent possessive pronoun "ours" is required, not the determiner "our."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "our," which must be followed by a noun (our proposal).
items.learningObjective: Use ours/theirs/mine when the possessive pronoun replaces a whole noun phrase.

items.question: If the company _____ the satellite office last year, commuting times would be shorter for many staff today.
items.explanation: This mixed conditional links a past unreal condition (had opened) to a present result (would be shorter).
items.commonMistake: Using second-conditional "opened," which would pair with a present/future hypothetical, not a past missed action.
items.learningObjective: Combine past perfect in the if-clause with would + base verb for present results of past unreal conditions.

items.question: The visitor parking lot _____ to be resurfaced during the holiday shutdown next month.
items.explanation: Future passive with "going to" uses "is/are going to be + past participle": is going to be resurfaced.
items.commonMistake: Reading "is going" as incomplete and rejecting it, or choosing active forms that ignore the passive marker "to be resurfaced."
items.learningObjective: Recognize be going to be + past participle as a planned future passive.

items.question: Customer ratings for the old checkout screen were _____ than those for the redesigned version.
items.explanation: When comparing two things with "than," use the comparative "worse," not the superlative "worst."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "worst," which is only correct when ranking three or more options without "than."
items.learningObjective: Use worse + than for a two-item negative comparison.

items.question: The warehouse processed _____ many returns this December as it did during last year's holiday peak.
items.explanation: The correlative structure is "as many … as." The blank needs "as" before "many."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "so" (so many … that) or "more" (more … than), which break the as…as pattern.
items.learningObjective: Recognize as many + noun + as for equal countable quantity.

items.question: The new distribution center is _____ than the old facility by nearly 20,000 square feet.
items.explanation: "Than" signals a comparative. "Larger" is the correct comparative form of "large."
items.commonMistake: Selecting the base adjective "large" or the superlative "largest" when "than" requires a comparative.
items.learningObjective: Use short-adjective -er form with than for size comparisons.

items.question: Oakdale Freight is one of the _____ dependable carriers the purchasing team has used this year.
items.explanation: After "one of the," use a superlative: "one of the most + adjective."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "more," which fits two-item comparisons with "than," not the "one of the …" pattern.
items.learningObjective: Use most (not more) after one of the + adjective.

items.question: The contractor signed _____ one-year maintenance agreement with the facilities department.
items.explanation: "One" begins with a /w/ consonant sound, so the indefinite article is "a," not "an."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "an" by looking at the vowel letter o instead of the spoken consonant sound.
items.learningObjective: Choose a/an by sound: a one-year… because one starts with /w/.

items.question: The steering committee will reconvene in _____ few weeks to finalize the vendor shortlist.
items.explanation: The fixed expression is "in a few weeks." "A few" means some (countable).
items.commonMistake: Omitting "a" or choosing "the few," which would imply a specific small group already identified.
items.learningObjective: Use a few for an indefinite small countable amount of time.

items.question: Staff may enter through _____ side door if the main lobby entrance is locked after 7:00 p.m.
items.explanation: "Either" means one or the other of two options and fits a singular noun ("side door").
items.commonMistake: Choosing "both" (needs plural) or "neither" (negative), which do not fit the permission context.
items.learningObjective: Use either + singular noun for one of two alternatives.

items.question: _____ employees attended the optional Saturday workshop, so the training room looked nearly empty.
items.explanation: "Few" without "a" emphasizes a surprisingly small number (almost none). That matches "nearly empty."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "A few," which suggests a small but positive attendance, conflicting with "nearly empty."
items.learningObjective: Distinguish few (negative scarcity) from a few (some, positive).

items.question: The finance team prepared a _____ overview of quarterly operating expenses for the board.
items.explanation: Before the noun "overview," the blank needs an adjective. "Detailed" modifies the noun.
items.commonMistake: Choosing the noun "detail/details" or the verb form "detailing" where an adjective is required.
items.learningObjective: Place an adjective immediately before the noun it modifies.

items.question: Leadership praised her _____ during the difficult contract renegotiation with the retailer.
items.explanation: After the possessive "her," the blank needs a noun. "Persistence" names the quality.
items.commonMistake: Selecting the adjective "persistent" or adverb "persistently" after a possessive determiner.
items.learningObjective: After possessive adjectives (her/his/their), use a noun.

items.question: The shuttle to the airport _____ every hour from the main lobby between 6:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.
items.explanation: Timetables and regular schedules use the simple present: "departs every hour."
items.commonMistake: Choosing past or perfect forms when a repeated schedule (every hour) requires simple present.
items.learningObjective: Use simple present for fixed schedules and timetables.

items.question: By next June, Ms. Ortega _____ for the company for twenty years.
items.explanation: "By next June" + duration "for twenty years" calls for future perfect continuous: will have been working.
items.commonMistake: Choosing present perfect "has worked" (no future anchor) or simple future "will work" (no duration emphasis).
items.learningObjective: Use will have been + -ing for duration up to a future point.

items.question: Tomorrow's webinar will focus _____ reducing energy costs across the retail store network.
items.explanation: The collocation is "focus on" + noun/gerund.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "in," "at," or "to," which are common but incorrect with "focus."
items.learningObjective: Memorize focus on as a fixed verb + preposition pair.

items.question: The regional team succeeded _____ closing three major accounts before the quarter ended.
items.explanation: "Succeed in" is followed by a gerund or noun: succeeded in closing…
items.commonMistake: Choosing "at" (good at) or "on," which do not collocate with "succeed."
items.learningObjective: Use succeed in + gerund for successful completion of an action.

items.question: _____ heavy traffic on the expressway, the courier reached the store before closing time.
items.explanation: "Despite" is followed by a noun phrase ("heavy traffic…"). "Although" would need a full clause.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "Although," which requires a subject + verb (Although traffic was heavy…), not a bare noun phrase.
items.learningObjective: Use despite + noun/gerund; use although + clause.

items.question: Investors praised the firm _____ packaging redesign cut shipping damage by 18 percent.
items.explanation: "Whose" links a noun to something it possesses: the firm whose packaging redesign…
items.commonMistake: Choosing "which" (no possessive) or "who" (people subject), neither of which shows ownership of "packaging redesign."
items.learningObjective: Use whose for possessive relative clauses with people or organizations.

items.question: _____ you need additional visitor badges, please notify the security desk before Friday.
items.explanation: Inverted first conditional: "Should you need…" = "If you need…." It expresses a possible future need.
items.commonMistake: Choosing "Had" (third conditional) or "Were" (second), which do not match a real future request.
items.learningObjective: Recognize Should + subject as an inverted first-conditional if-clause.

items.question: Customer satisfaction surveys _____ by an independent research firm every spring.
items.explanation: The surveys receive the action, so use present simple passive: are conducted (+ by-agent).
items.commonMistake: Choosing active "conduct" or progressive "are conducting," which would need the research firm as subject.
items.learningObjective: Use am/is/are + past participle for present simple passive with habitual by-agents.

items.question: Most clerks _____ rather finish the inventory count tonight than return on Saturday morning.
items.explanation: The preference idiom is "would rather + base verb (+ than…)."
items.commonMistake: Choosing "should" or "must," which express advice/obligation rather than preference.
items.learningObjective: Use would rather + base verb to express preference.

items.question: Neither of the finalists _____ experience managing a multilingual support center.
items.explanation: "Neither of + plural noun" takes a singular verb in formal workplace English: neither… has.
items.commonMistake: Agreeing with the plural "finalists" and choosing "have," which is common in casual speech but not preferred on TOEIC.
items.learningObjective: Treat neither of as singular for verb agreement in exam English.
